hero.caption: The restored Johnson Farm in Bedford County, Virginia, occupied by the Johnsons from 1854 to the early 1940s. It is one of the only remaining buildings from the community that flourished in the Peaks of Otter area. It existed as a four-room log cabin when John T. Johnson bought the farm in 1852.

images.caption: The Peaks of Otter area is named for three mountain peaks – Sharp Top, Flat Top, and Harkening Hill – in the Blue Ridge Mountains. The area is also home to its namesake Peaks of Otter salamander. Credit: Meagan Racey/USFWS
images.alt: The Peaks of Otter area is named for three mountain peaks – Sharp Top, Flat Top, and Harkening Hill – in the Blue Ridge Mountains. The area is also home to its namesake Peaks of Otter salamander. Credit: Meagan Racey/USFWS
images.artist: U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service - Northeast Region

images.caption: Liberty University biology professor Norman Reichenbach holds a Peaks of Otter salamander. The species was first described in 1957 by Gordon Thurow. It is a slender, lungless woodland salamander that is dark brown with abundant brassy metallic spots or blotches. Adults grow up to nearly 2.5 inches and can live up to 10 years in the wild. Credit: Meagan Racey/USFWS

images.caption: The Peaks of Otter salamander has no lungs, breathing entirely through the tissues in its mouth and skin. Preserving adequate tree cover to prevent the sun from drying soil and leaf litter is crucial as the salamander relies on adequate ground moisture to keep its skin moist enough to breathe and to forage successfully in the forest. Through a conservation agreement with U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, U.S. Forest Service and National Park Service, timber harvest is managed to ensure habitat and canopy cover remain intact. Credit: Meagan Racey/USFWS

images.caption: Wendi Weber, the Fish and Wildlife Service North Atlantic-Appalachian regional director, holds a Peaks of Otter salamander. The salamander joins the ranks of more than 190 other species in the eastern U.S. whose populations have been determined to be stable thanks to research and conservation by federal, tribal, state, private and non-governmental partners. The effort to conserve at-risk wildlife and recover listed species is led by the Fish and Wildlife Service and state wildlife agencies in coordination with many other entities. Partners commit to finding solutions that keep working lands working and conserve wildlife and their habitats, such that some at-risk species may avoid becoming threatened or endangered at all. Credit: Meagan Racey/USFWS
